narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 68.8% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The three factors that weighed most heavily against you were your class ranking in your third year of law school, your first-year class ranking, and your family income bracket. All three pushed the model toward predicting failure rather than success.

Your third-year ranking placed you in the fourth decile—noticeably lower than the average of accepted students (just under the sixth decile). This was the single strongest reason the model expected you to struggle on the bar. Your first-year ranking was also below the typical accepted student (fourth decile versus sixth), adding further concern. Finally, coming from an upper-middle-income family worked against you; while many accepted applicants share this background, the model learned that this bracket, when combined with the other academic signals, slightly increased the estimated risk of bar failure.

Taken together, these academic performance indicators outweighed your solid LSAT and GPA, which were only marginally below the averages of accepted students.

You should focus on strengthening your academic record and bar-exam readiness. Consider retaking key courses, enrolling in a structured bar-preparation program, or gaining additional practical legal experience before reapplying. These steps can directly address the areas the model flagged as weakest. (218 words)
